title: Affiliate Marketing
hook: FE shows an affiliate-program flow and asks which arrow is which step. Learn the sequence.
model: In **affiliate marketing**, a site owner (affiliate) posts an advertiser's ad or link.
The advertiser pays the affiliate a **success fee** (commission) only when a referred visitor buys (or completes an action).
It is pay-for-results: no sale, no fee.
Money flows **advertiser → affiliate**; the purchase goes **viewer → advertiser**.

example.q: A blogger joins a bookstore's affiliate program. Trace one sale.
steps: Blogger joins and puts the bookstore's ad on the blog.
A reader clicks the ad and lands on the bookstore's product page.
The reader buys the book from the bookstore.
The bookstore pays the blogger a commission based on that sale.

checks.q: Order the steps of an affiliate program.
steps: Site owner joins the advertiser's affiliate program
Visitor clicks the ad on the site
Visitor is taken to the advertiser's sales page
Visitor buys the product
Advertiser pays the site owner a success fee
checks.why: Join → click → link → buy → commission. The fee comes last because it depends on the sale.

checks.q: In an affiliate program, who pays whom the success fee?
opts: The visitor pays the site owner
The advertiser (EC site) pays the site owner
The site owner pays the advertiser
checks.why: The advertiser rewards the affiliate site for the sale it referred. The visitor pays only for the product itself.

trap: Mixing up the purchase (viewer → EC site) with the success fee (EC site → site owner).

title: Balanced Scorecard
hook: FE gives a target + KPI and asks which of the 4 BSC perspectives it belongs to.
model: A **BSC** turns strategy into targets and **KPIs** across 4 perspectives.
**Financial**: profit, sales growth, ROI.
**Customer**: satisfaction, retention, complaints.
**Internal business process**: efficiency and quality inside operations (lead time, defect rate).
**Learning & growth**: people and capability (training, skills).

example.q: Target: faster production. KPI: fewer days to manufacture. Which perspective?
steps: It measures how operations run inside the firm.
Not money, not customers, not training → **internal business process**.

checks.q: Put each KPI in its BSC perspective.
items: Operating profit margin
Repeat-customer rate
Defect rate on the line
Hours of staff skills training
checks.why: Classify by what is measured: money, customers, operations, or staff capability.

checks.q: Target: shorten order-to-shipment time. KPI: average processing days. Which perspective?
checks.why: Processing time measures how efficiently internal operations run.

trap: Calling training for development capability "internal process"; training staff is learning & growth.

title: Benchmarking
hook: Benchmarking appears alongside BPR, ERP and core competence. The word to look for is **comparison**.
model: **Benchmarking**: compare your own products, services and processes with **competitors or best-practice (advanced) companies**.
The comparison is both qualitative and quantitative. You find the gap, then copy or adapt the better practice.
**BPR** is something else: a radical redesign of business processes, using IT, from the customer's view.
**Core competence**: putting resources into your unique, hard-to-copy skills.

example.q: A bank finds its loan approval takes 10 days while the best rival takes 2. It studies the rival's process. What is this?
steps: It measures its own process against a top performer.
It finds the gap (10 vs 2 days) and learns from the better practice.
This is **benchmarking**.

checks.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Compare yourself with leading firms to find gaps
Radically redesign business processes using IT
Focus on unique skills rivals can't easily copy
checks.why: Only benchmarking is built on comparison with others. The other three are about redesign, focus and integration.

checks.q: A hotel measures its check-in time and guest ratings against the top chain in the region. What is this?
checks.why: Measuring against a best-in-class company is benchmarking.

trap: The BPR option (redesigning processes from the customer's view with IT) sounds like improvement, but it involves no comparison.

title: Role of the CIO
hook: FE often asks what the CIO does. The answer is always strategy-level, company-wide IT planning.
model: The **CIO** (chief information officer) is the top executive responsible for information systems.
Main job: build **information/IT strategy** aligned with business strategy and optimize IT investment across the whole company.
Not a day-to-day manager of the IT department, and not the **system auditor**, who must be independent.
Needs both IT knowledge and business/industry knowledge.

example.q: Which is the CIO's task: (1) fix a server outage, (2) audit system controls, (3) plan company-wide IT investment for a new business strategy?
steps: (1) is operations work for IT staff.
(2) is done by an independent auditor.
(3) is strategic and company-wide → **CIO**.

checks.q: Which is a major responsibility of the CIO?
opts: Auditing whether systems work properly and advising the IT department
Creating a company-wide plan to get the most from IT investment in support of business strategy
Answering user queries about the system and assigning fixes
Running daily backups for the data center
checks.why: The CIO's role is strategic: aligning IT investment with business strategy. Auditing and daily operations belong to others.

checks.q: Match each role to its main concern.
pairs: Keeping systems running day to day
checks.why: Strategy belongs to the CIO, independent assurance to the auditor, and running systems to operations.

trap: Choosing the option about giving detailed improvement instructions; that is operational management, not the CIO's strategic role.

title: Facilitator
hook: The exam asks for the facilitator's role. The key word is **neutral**.
model: A **facilitator** runs the meeting process from a **neutral, impartial** position.
Gets **everyone to speak**, draws out opinions, and organizes the flow of discussion toward agreement.
Does **not** push a conclusion (not even management's).
Is not the clerk (schedule, materials, minutes) and not a subject expert giving advice.

example.q: In a requirements workshop, the sales head talks over everyone. What should the facilitator do?
steps: Stay neutral and don't take sides.
Invite quieter members to share their views.
Summarize the points so far and guide the group to the next topic.

checks.q: Which behavior fits a facilitator?
opts: Steering the group to the answer the boss wants
Asking silent members for their views and summarizing the discussion without taking sides
Booking the room and writing the minutes
checks.why: Facilitators stay impartial and help everyone take part. The other options are a biased chair, an admin role and an expert role.

checks.q: Is it the facilitator's job?
items: Encourage all participants to speak
Organize the flow of discussion
Lead the group to management's preferred decision
Prepare handouts and take minutes
checks.why: The facilitator handles the discussion process neutrally. Pushing a decision breaks neutrality, and admin work belongs to a secretary.

trap: "Acting as chair and controlling the talk to reach management's conclusion" sounds like leadership, but it breaks neutrality.

title: Cause and Effect (Fishbone) Diagram
hook: You may be shown part of the diagram and asked how two boxes are related. A bone that points into a line is a **cause** of it.
model: One of the **seven QC tools**. Also called the Ishikawa or **fishbone** diagram.
The **effect** (problem) sits at the head. The spine points to it.
Big bones are main cause groups. Smaller bones are sub-causes that point into the bigger ones.
Common cause groups are the **4M**: Man, Machine, Method, Material.
Different from a logic tree (purpose → means) and a Pareto chart (ranks items by size).

example.q: Head: "Late deliveries". A bone "Truck breakdowns" points into the spine, and "No maintenance schedule" points into the "Truck breakdowns" bone. Relationships?
steps: Truck breakdowns point into the spine, so they are a cause of late deliveries.
No maintenance schedule points into the breakdown bone, so it is a cause of the breakdowns.
It is a chain of causes ending at the effect.

checks.q: In a fishbone diagram, a small bone X points into a larger bone Y. What is X to Y?
checks.why: Every bone shows a cause, pointing toward the effect it contributes to.

checks.q: Match each QC tool to what it shows.
pairs: Items sorted by size with a cumulative line
checks.why: The fishbone organizes causes. The Pareto chart ranks how big each item is. The scatter diagram shows correlation.

trap: "B is the means of A" describes a logic/tree diagram. In a fishbone diagram, a bone is always a cause.

title: Franchising vs Licensing
hook: Both involve royalties. The difference is whether the partner **runs a store under your rules with your support**.
model: **Franchising**: independent owners (franchisees) invest in and run their own stores under the franchisor's **brand and standards**.
The franchisee pays **royalties** for the brand **and** business support (training, know-how, supply).
**Licensing**: the right to use IP (a trademark, patent or technology) for a royalty, with no store-operation rules or support package.
**Direct distribution**: the maker sells straight to consumers. **Wholesaling**: selling in bulk to retailers or businesses.

example.q: A milk-tea brand lets an entrepreneur open a shop with her own money. She follows the brand's recipes and store rules, gets training, and pays a monthly royalty. What is this?
steps: She is an independent owner who invests her own money.
She uses the brand under its standards and gets support.
She pays royalties, so this is **franchising**.

checks.q: A toy maker pays a film studio a royalty to print a movie character on its own products. The studio sets no store rules and gives no business support. What is this?
checks.why: Paying only for the right to use IP, with no operating rules or support, is licensing.

checks.q: Which arrangement does each feature point to?
items: Owner must follow store management rules
Franchisor provides training and support
Royalty only for using a patent
Use of a trademark on your own product line
checks.why: Operating rules plus support mean franchising. Using IP alone means licensing.

trap: Licensing also involves royalties, but it covers only the use of IP or a brand, without store-operation duties or support.

title: Green Procurement
hook: A quick definition question: spot the option about **buying** eco-friendly goods, not certificates or labels.
model: **Green procurement** (green purchasing): when buying, consider **environmental burden** on top of quality and price.
Prefer products and services with a lower environmental impact, from **suppliers** that work to reduce their own impact.
It is a **purchasing** decision by the buyer (company or government).
Not the same as **eco-labels** (third-party certified product labels) or tradable **green power certificates**.

example.q: A city office is buying printers. Two models match on price and quality, but one uses less power and its maker runs an emissions-cut program. What does green procurement say?
steps: Quality and price are tied, so look at environmental burden.
Model 2 has lower impact and a greener supplier.
Buy model 2. That choice is green procurement.

checks.q: Which activity is green procurement?
opts: Buying recycled paper from a vendor with an environmental program, when quality and price are acceptable
Getting a third-party eco-label for your own product
Raising investor funds for tree planting
checks.why: Green procurement is about what the organization **buys**. Labels, power certificates and fundraising are other environmental schemes.

checks.q: Sort each item.
items: Choosing low-energy servers when quality and price are similar
Preferring suppliers that cut their CO_{2} emissions
An eco-label standard certified by a third party
Trading green power certificates
checks.why: Only purchase decisions belong to green procurement. Labels and certificates are separate tools.

trap: An option about third-party environmental labels (ISO 14020 family) sounds green, but it describes eco-labels, not procurement.

title: HR Systems: Work Sharing and Friends
hook: FE describes an HR scheme in one line and asks you to name it.
model: **Work sharing**: shorten each employee's hours so the work is spread across more people, protecting or creating jobs.
**Cafeteria plan**: employees pick the benefits they want from a menu, within a set budget or points.
**Free-agent system**: employees apply to move to the department or job they want.
**Work-life balance**: harmony between work and personal life (family, health, growth).

example.q: A factory facing a slump cuts everyone's hours by 20% instead of laying off 20% of staff. Which system?
steps: Total work is split among more people by reducing hours per person.
Jobs are kept → **work sharing**.

checks.q: Match each HR system to its description.
pairs: Fewer hours per worker to keep or create jobs
Choose your own benefits from a menu
Apply yourself to transfer to a desired post
Harmony between job and private life
checks.why: Each name describes its mechanism: share hours, pick benefits like a cafeteria, act as a free agent, balance life.

checks.q: Which aims to keep employment across society by cutting working hours per person?
checks.why: Work sharing spreads the available work over more workers. Work-life balance is about personal well-being, not spreading jobs.

trap: Choosing work-life balance because it mentions hours; its goal is personal harmony, not spreading jobs.

title: IoT System Elements
hook: FE gives an IoT table (collection, transmission, analysis, utilization) and asks which device fits which stage.
model: **Data collection**: sensors on things (temperature, vibration, cameras).
**Data transmission**: networks that carry data (wireless LAN, LPWA, gateways).
**Data analysis**: software/cloud/AI that judges the data (e.g., detects abnormal values).
**Data utilization**: acting on results (dashboards, alerts, instructions to workers, actuators).

example.q: A smart farm: soil-moisture probe → Wi-Fi → cloud model decides it's too dry → sprinkler turns on. Label each.
steps: Probe = collection.
Wi-Fi = transmission.
Cloud model = analysis.
Sprinkler action = utilization.

checks.q: Match each IoT stage to an example in a smart building.
pairs: Software that flags unusual power use
Screen telling staff which room to check
checks.why: Sensors gather, the network carries, software judges, and the display/action uses the result.

checks.q: In an IoT setup for equipment maintenance, which item belongs to data collection?
opts: Vibration sensor mounted on a motor
checks.why: Collection is done by sensors at the equipment. The others are transmission, analysis, and utilization.

trap: Choosing the wireless link for collection; it only transmits data, it doesn't sense it.

title: M&A and the Synergy Effect
hook: FE describes what a merged company does and asks you to name the effect. Combined value > sum of parts = synergy.
model: **Synergy effect**: 1 + 1 > 2. The combined firm creates more value than both could alone.
Sources: cross-selling (revenue), shared technology, and cutting duplicate costs (offices, systems).
**Horizontal integration**: merging with a firm at the same stage (e.g., a competitor).
**Vertical integration**: merging along the supply chain (a supplier or distributor).

example.q: Bakery chain A buys rival bakery chain B, sells A's cakes in B's shops, and closes one of two head offices.
steps: Same business, same stage → the deal type is **horizontal integration**.
Extra sales plus saved head-office cost = value beyond the two alone → **synergy effect**.

checks.q: Match each term to its description.
pairs: Combined firm earns more than the two separately
Acquiring a competitor at the same stage
checks.why: Synergy is the value effect; horizontal and vertical integration describe the deal's direction.

checks.q: After a merger, the new firm shares R&D results and merges duplicate IT systems, earning more than both firms did alone. What is this called?
checks.why: The question asks for the value-creating phenomenon, not the type of merger.

trap: Choosing horizontal/vertical integration. These name the merger type, not the extra value it creates.

title: MOT: Product vs Process Innovation
hook: FE asks you to tell product innovation from process innovation, and both from MOT itself.
model: **MOT** (management of technology): running the business with technology as a core strategic resource.
**Product innovation**: creating new products, or products clearly differentiated from competitors'.
**Process innovation**: radically improving **how** work is done (production, logistics, business processes).
Quick test: changes **what you sell** = product; changes **how you make/deliver it** = process.

example.q: A phone maker releases the first foldable-screen model, then automates its assembly line to halve build time. Classify each.
steps: Foldable model = a new, differentiated thing to sell → **product innovation**.
Automated line = same product, better way of making it → **process innovation**.

checks.q: Sort each change into the right type of innovation.
items: Launching an EV with a new battery design
A bank adding a never-before-offered savings app
Switching a warehouse to robot picking
Redesigning order processing to cut lead time
checks.why: New or differentiated offerings are product innovation; better ways of producing or operating are process innovation.

checks.q: A firm treats its patents and R&D as the center of corporate strategy and manages them strategically. This describes:
checks.why: Managing the business with technology as its core is the definition of MOT itself, not one kind of innovation.

trap: Picking "innovative reform of business processes" for product innovation; that is process innovation.

title: MRP: Material Requirements Planning
hook: FE expects you to know MRP computes how many parts to order from the production plan, and not to confuse it with build-to-order.
model: **MRP** works out the quantity and timing of components/materials needed.
Inputs: the **master production schedule** (what to build, when), the **bill of materials** (parts per product), and **inventory** data.
**Net requirement** = gross requirement − stock on hand (− parts already on order).
It is plan-driven: production follows the schedule, not individual customer orders.

example.q: Plan: 200 tables. Each table needs 4 legs. 300 legs are in stock. How many legs to order?
steps: Gross requirement = 200 × 4 = 800 legs.
Net requirement = 800 − 300 = **500 legs**.

checks.q: The plan calls for 150 chairs. Each chair needs 3 casters. 120 casters are in stock and none are on order. How many casters must be ordered?
Which statement best describes MRP?
opts: Production starts only after a customer order arrives
Component quantities are calculated from the production plan and the bill of materials
Design and production preparation run in parallel to shorten development
Work and transport instructions travel on a card attached to parts
checks.why: MRP explodes the production plan through the BOM. The others are build-to-order, concurrent engineering, and kanban.

checks.q: Put the MRP calculation in order.
steps: Take the master production schedule
Explode it with the bill of materials into gross requirements
Subtract inventory to get net requirements
Issue orders for the net quantity
checks.why: MRP goes plan → gross parts → net of stock → orders.

trap: "Production starts after the customer order" is build-to-order, not MRP.

title: OC Curve (Sampling Inspection)
hook: FE asks how an OC curve shifts when the acceptance number C or the sample size n changes.
model: An **OC curve** plots lot **percent defective** (x-axis) against the **probability the lot is accepted** (y-axis).
Take n samples; accept the lot if the number of defectives is ≤ **C** (acceptance number).
Larger C is more lenient: the curve sits higher and falls later. **C = 0 is the strictest** (lowest curve).
With C fixed, a larger n makes the curve steeper (sharper discrimination).

example.q: n = 2, C = 0, lot is 20% defective. P(accept)?
steps: Accept only if both samples are good.

checks.q: Sample n = 2 items, accept if 0 defectives (C = 0). Lot is 10% defective. Probability the lot is accepted? (decimal)
checks.why: Each item is good with p = 0.9, so P = 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81.

checks.q: Three sampling plans use the same sample size but acceptance numbers C = 1, 3, 5. Whose OC curve is highest (accepts most easily)?
checks.why: Allowing more defectives makes acceptance easier at any defect rate, so C = 5 is the outermost curve and C = 1 the innermost.

checks.q: n = 2, C = 1, lot 10% defective. P(accept)? (decimal)
checks.why: Reject only if both are defective: 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01. So P(accept) = 1 − 0.01 = 0.99.

trap: Thinking C = 0 is the most lenient and drawing it outermost; it is the strictest, so it is the lowest curve.

title: Pricing Methods
hook: Each pricing method starts from a different anchor: cost, competitors, a profit target, or the customer. Find the anchor and you have the answer.
model: **Cost-plus pricing**: price = cost (manufacturing or purchase) + a set margin.
**Competition-based (going-rate) pricing**: follow the industry average or rivals' prices.
**Target-return pricing**: set the price so a target profit is earned at a planned sales volume.
**Perceived-value (customer-based) pricing**: price at what customers accept for the quality, found by research.

example.q: A shop buys a bag for ₱800 and adds a 25% margin on cost. What is the cost-plus price?

checks.q: A unit costs ₱1,200 to make. With cost-plus pricing at a 15% margin on cost, what is the price?
Match each method to its anchor.
pairs: Target profit at a planned volume
checks.why: Name the starting point of the price and you name the method.

trap: Target-return pricing also covers costs, but it is built around a planned sales volume and profit goal, not a simple margin on cost.

title: Process vs Product Innovation
hook: Ask yourself: is the new thing **what** is made, or **how** it is made?
model: **Process innovation**: a new or much better **way of making or delivering** something (new procedures, automation), often for higher quality or lower cost.
**Product innovation**: a new or much better **product or service** itself.
Outsourcing production to another company is not innovation in itself.
Becoming a **de facto standard** is market adoption, not a type of innovation.

example.q: A bakery keeps the same bread but adds a new oven control method that cuts burnt loaves from 8% to 1%. What kind of innovation is this?
steps: The product (the bread) is unchanged.
The production procedure is new and improves quality.
This is **process innovation**.

checks.q: Sort each item.
items: A new assembly method that cuts defects
Robots that speed up packing in the warehouse
Launching a foldable smartphone
A new flavor of instant noodles
checks.why: Changing **how** goods are made or handled is process innovation. A new item for sale is product innovation.

checks.q: Which is process innovation?
opts: Inventing a brand-new drug using original technology
Introducing a new production procedure that raises product quality
Hiring another firm to do the manufacturing
Your format winning the market and becoming a de facto standard
checks.why: Only the new production procedure changes how the product is made.

trap: "An innovative new product based on high technology" is product innovation, not process innovation.

title: Product Life Cycle
hook: You get a description of a market and must name the stage. Growth and maturity are the usual mix-up.
model: 4 stages: **Introduction → Growth → Maturity → Decline**.
**Introduction**: few buyers, demand must be created, high promotion cost, little or no profit.
**Growth**: the market starts to see the value, **sales rise fast**, competitors enter, invest to widen **product lines and channels**.
**Maturity**: demand **peaks**, competition is hardest, differentiation, segmentation, cost cutting.
**Decline**: demand falls, some firms exit, decide to stay, harvest or move to another market.

example.q: Smartwatch sales doubled this year. More brands are joining and the maker is opening new store channels. Which stage?
steps: Sales rising fast, so not introduction (small) and not maturity (flat peak).
New competitors are joining and the firm is investing in channels.
Answer: **growth** stage.

checks.q: Put the product life cycle stages in order.
steps: Introduction
Growth
Maturity
Decline
checks.why: A product is launched, gains acceptance, peaks, then fades.

checks.q: Match each stage to its typical situation.
pairs: Sales climb; expand lines and channels
Demand peaks; fierce competition and cost cutting
checks.why: Each stage is defined by where demand is heading and how many competitors are in the market.

trap: Peak demand with fierce competition is maturity, not growth. Growth means sales are still climbing.

title: Relationship Marketing
hook: Keywords: a **long-term** relationship with each customer, giving stable sales over time.
model: **Relationship marketing**: build and keep good long-term relationships with each customer.
The goal is stable, repeated sales from the same customer over time (retention).
Typical tools: loyalty programs, after-sales follow-up, CRM data.
Not the same as one-off tactics like flash sales, location-based ads, or a **media mix** (using TV, print and other media together).

example.q: A coffee chain gives app members a free drink every 10th visit and a birthday greeting, and tracks their favorite orders. Which approach?
steps: The aim is to keep the same customers coming back for years.
It strengthens each customer relationship.
This is **relationship marketing**.

checks.q: Which is relationship marketing?
opts: Ads sent to phones near a store via GPS
Keeping in touch with each customer to win repeat sales for years
Running the same campaign on TV, radio and newspapers
checks.why: Relationship marketing aims for long-term repeat sales per customer. The others are short-term or channel tactics.

checks.q: Sort each tactic.
items: Loyalty points program
Personal after-sales follow-up calls
Using several media at once
Time-limited flash sale
checks.why: Long-term retention tools are relationship marketing. Media mix and flash sales aim at reach or quick sales.

trap: "Reaching consumers through TV, newspapers and magazines" is a media mix, not relationship marketing.

title: RFID (IC Tags)
hook: FE asks for RFID's key traits: contactless radio reading, readable through packaging, and resistant to dirt.
model: An **RFID / IC tag** is a small IC chip plus antenna, read and written by **radio waves** without contact.
No line of sight needed: tags can be read through boxes or packaging, and several at once.
Resistant to dirt and stains, unlike barcodes, which must be visible and clean.
Passive tags get their power from the reader's radio waves, so they need no battery.

example.q: A warehouse must count 50 sealed cartons on a pallet. Barcode or RFID?
steps: Barcodes need each label visible and scanned one by one.
RFID tags are read by radio through the cartons, many at once → **RFID**.

checks.q: Which technology has each trait?
items: Read by radio waves without contact
Can be read through packaging
Must be in the scanner's line of sight
Swiped or inserted into a magnetic reader
checks.why: Contactless radio reading is RFID. Barcodes are optical, so they need line of sight. Magnetic stripes need physical contact with a reader.

checks.q: Which is a characteristic of RFID tags?
opts: They must be inserted into a dedicated magnetic reader
Their data can be read without contact, even through the package
They store their data on an external hard disk
checks.why: RFID is read wirelessly by radio, so contact and visibility aren't needed.

trap: Picking "insert into a magnetic reader"; that describes magnetic-stripe cards.

title: Sharing Economy
hook: Look for **individuals** sharing **unused assets** through an online platform.
model: **Sharing economy**: mostly between individuals, people **share, lend or rent out idle assets** (rooms, cars, tools, skills).
An online platform or social media matches the people and builds trust (ratings, reviews).
Examples: room sharing (Airbnb-type), car and ride sharing.
Not a **smart city** (IT running energy and city infrastructure) and not **omnichannel** (joining in-store and online sales).

example.q: Ana rents out her spare room and her rarely used car to strangers through an app with reviews. What model is this?
steps: The assets belong to an individual and would otherwise sit unused.
A platform connects her with other individuals.
This is the **sharing economy**.

checks.q: Match each concept to its description.
pairs: Individuals lend unused assets through a platform
IT manages energy and urban infrastructure
Store and online sales combined into one experience
checks.why: Only the sharing economy is about individuals putting idle assets to use.

checks.q: Which is an example of the sharing economy?
opts: A city using sensors to control streetlights
A retailer letting you buy online and pick up in store
Neighbors renting out idle power tools through an app
checks.why: Individuals lending idle assets to each other through a platform is the sharing economy.

trap: The smart-city option (IT for renewable energy and urban infrastructure) sounds modern and sustainable, but nothing is being shared.

title: Total Quality Management (TQM)
hook: FE asks which statement is part of TQM. Look for the customer focus and company-wide involvement.
model: **TQM**: company-wide quality management in which every department and employee takes part.
Goal: **customer satisfaction**, i.e., products/services that meet or exceed customer expectations.
Continuous improvement (PDCA) and decisions based on data.
Favors employee **empowerment** and cross-department cooperation, not top-down control or departments competing.

example.q: A firm says: "Each department optimizes its own quality targets, competing with the others." Is this TQM?
steps: TQM is company-wide and cooperative.
Departments competing independently goes against that → **not TQM**.

checks.q: Does each practice fit TQM?
items: Designing services around customer expectations
All employees joining improvement activities
Only top management may make quality decisions
Departments compete instead of cooperating
checks.why: TQM is customer-focused, company-wide, and empowering. Central control and silos go against it.

checks.q: Which is part of TQM?
opts: Hiring only staff with long experience in similar firms
Products and services that meet or exceed customer expectations
Centralizing every quality decision at headquarters
Letting each department pursue its own goals independently
checks.why: TQM starts and ends with the customer.

trap: Picking centralized decision-making because it "ensures quality"; TQM relies on empowered employees.

title: Training Methods
hook: You get a description of a training activity and must name it. Learn the key picture for each method.
model: **In-basket**: work through a pile of simulated tasks (memos, orders, expense forms) **within a time limit**.
**Role-playing**: act out a role (e.g., interviewer and customer) and practice interpersonal skills.
**Case study**: analyze a real or realistic business case and discuss solutions.
**OJT**: a supervisor teaches skills during actual daily work. **Off-JT**: classroom-style training away from the job.

example.q: Trainees get 60 minutes to clear an inbox of 15 items: reply to a complaint, approve a purchase order, and file a travel claim. Which method?
steps: Many simulated tasks to handle.
A fixed time limit.
Pile of paperwork plus a timer means **in-basket**.

checks.q: Match each method to its description.
pairs: Process many simulated tasks within a time limit
Act out a part, such as interviewer or customer
Analyze a business case and discuss solutions
Learn from a supervisor during real work
checks.why: Each method has one signature feature: a timed task pile, acting, case analysis, or learning on the real job.

checks.q: New staff pair up. One acts as an angry customer and the other practices calming them down. Which method?
checks.why: Acting out interpersonal roles is role-playing. In-basket is about handling a pile of tasks.

trap: Role-playing also simulates work, but it means acting out people roles. A timed pile of tasks is in-basket.

title: Business Process Reengineering (BPR)
hook: BPR = **rebuild** the process from scratch for dramatic gains. It is not just automating what already exists.
model: **BPR**: fundamentally redesign business processes (and the organization if needed) for dramatic gains in productivity, cost, service and quality.
It starts from analyzing the business content and flow, then redesigns toward targets such as profit or customer satisfaction.
Compare **kaizen**: small, continuous improvements, not radical change.
Compare **BPM**: an ongoing cycle of managing and improving processes. **SFA**: automates sales activities.
Simply putting today's process onto a computer is automation, not BPR.

example.q: A bank's loan approval passes through 6 departments and takes 3 weeks. What would BPR do?
steps: Question why 6 hand-offs are needed at all.
Redesign: one case team, backed by a shared system, handles the whole application.
Approval drops to 2 days. This is radical redesign, so it's **BPR**.

checks.q: Which is BPR?
opts: Scanning the same paper forms so they're stored digitally
Scrapping a 5-step approval chain and redesigning the whole process around one team
Holding monthly kaizen meetings for small fixes
Installing an SFA tool for sales reps
checks.why: BPR rethinks and restructures the process itself for dramatic results. The others digitize, tweak or support existing work.

checks.q: Radical or incremental?
items: Merging departments and redesigning order fulfilment end to end
Automating an existing form without changing steps
Continuous small improvements by workers
Rebuilding the claims process so one person handles a case start to finish
checks.why: BPR changes the process structure fundamentally. Automation of the old process and kaizen do not.

trap: Automating key processes to save time sounds like BPR, but without redesigning the process it is just automation.

title: DFD, E-R & UML for Business Modeling
hook: FE describes a diagram style and asks which modeling technique it is. Learn the signature of each.
model: **DFD**: shows how **data flows** between processes, data stores and external entities (sources/sinks). It shows data only, not goods or money.
In a DFD every process has both an input and an output data flow.
**E-R diagram**: data-oriented. It shows entities, their attributes and the relationships between them. Structure, not flow.
**UML**: a set of standard object-modeling notations with several purpose-specific diagrams (e.g. use case, activity, class, sequence) that show a process from **multiple viewpoints**.

example.q: An order clerk receives an order from a customer, checks stock in the inventory file, and sends shipping info to the warehouse. Which diagram shows this information movement?
steps: Customer and warehouse are external entities (source/sink).
"Check stock" is a process, and the inventory file is a data store.
Arrows carry order and shipping data, so this is a **DFD**.

checks.q: Match the DFD symbol to its meaning.
pairs: Source or destination of data outside the system
Transforms input data into output data
Where data is kept, like a file
checks.why: These four symbols are all a DFD uses, and exam questions often test their meanings.

checks.q: A team models a business with a use case diagram, an activity diagram and a class diagram, all in standard object notation. What are they using?
checks.why: Several purpose-specific diagrams in standardized object-modeling notation is the signature of UML.

trap: DFD = data **moving** between processes. E-R = data **structure** (entities and relationships). Don't swap them.

title: SaaS & Hybrid Cloud
hook: Know what each service model takes off your hands, what it does **not**, and what makes a cloud "hybrid".
model: **SaaS**: the provider builds and runs the application, and you just use it over the network. No app development for you.
**PaaS**: the provider gives a platform (OS, middleware, runtime), and you build your own apps on it. **IaaS**: the provider gives servers, storage and network, and you manage the rest.
Even with SaaS, the user still owns access management (IDs, passwords), security rules, and procedures for failures and data backup.
**Private cloud**: for one company's exclusive use. **Public cloud**: general-purpose, shared by many customers.
**Hybrid cloud**: private and public clouds are **linked** so data and apps work across both.

example.q: A company uses a cloud email service it did not build. What service model is it, and what must it still do?
steps: The provider supplies and runs the finished application, so it is **SaaS**.
The company skips development and server/log design.
It must still manage user accounts and passwords, set security rules, and plan what to do during an outage.

checks.q: Match each model to what the provider supplies.
pairs: A platform to run your own apps
checks.why: Going from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the provider takes on more layers, and SaaS covers everything up to the application.

checks.q: Which setup is a hybrid cloud?
opts: A public cloud split into free and paid plans
A company's private cloud linked with a public cloud so apps share data
Customizing a SaaS screen for one company
One cloud service sold to both consumers and businesses
checks.why: Hybrid means combining and linking an exclusive (private) cloud with a general-purpose (public) cloud.

trap: Don't assume SaaS removes **all** duties. Access control, security rules and failure/backup procedures stay with the user.

title: Feasibility Study
hook: Know what each feasibility type asks. The exam names a concern and asks which type it belongs to.
model: **Economic feasibility**: do lifetime **benefits exceed lifetime costs**? (cost-benefit analysis)
**Technical feasibility**: can it be built with available technology and skills?
**Operational feasibility**: will users and the organization actually be able to run and accept it?
**Schedule feasibility**: can it be finished within the required time?

example.q: A new system costs ₱5M over 5 years and is expected to save ₱7M. Which feasibility is being checked?
steps: We are comparing money in vs money out over the system's life.
₱7M benefit > ₱5M cost, so it passes.
That is **economic feasibility**.

checks.q: Match the concern to the feasibility type.
pairs: Savings over 5 years outweigh total costs
Our servers can handle the required load
Branch staff can use it without major retraining
Can go live before the new tax law takes effect
checks.why: Money = economic, technology = technical, people and work fit = operational, deadline = schedule.

checks.q: Staff may resist a new system because it changes their daily routine. Which feasibility covers this?
checks.why: Whether users will accept and run the system in daily work is operational feasibility.

trap: Operational feasibility is about people using the system, not costs vs benefits.

title: Green IT
hook: Pick the option that clearly **cuts energy use or CO_{2}**, not one that just sounds efficient or powerful.
model: **Green IT** reduces the environmental impact of IT and uses IT to reduce society's impact.
**Green of IT**: make IT itself save energy, e.g. energy-efficient servers, virtualization to cut machine count, thin clients.
**Green by IT**: use IT to save resources elsewhere, e.g. web conferencing instead of travel, telework, paperless workflows.

example.q: Which is Green IT: buying more powerful servers, or merging 20 servers into 4 via virtualization?
steps: More powerful servers do not necessarily lower energy use.
Consolidating to 4 physical machines cuts power and cooling needs.
Virtualization consolidation is **Green IT**.

checks.q: Which is the best example of Green IT?
opts: Building a larger in-house data center
Replacing thin clients with desktop PCs
Holding online meetings instead of flying staff to meetings
checks.why: Online meetings avoid travel emissions. That is a direct environmental benefit through IT.

checks.q: Sort into Green-of-IT (greener IT itself) and Green-by-IT (IT greens other activities).
items: Server virtualization
Telework
Paperless e-approval workflow
Low-power data center cooling
checks.why: Making IT equipment use less energy is green of IT. Using IT to replace travel or paper is green by IT.

trap: "Efficient software" sounds green, but the exam wants a clear energy/CO_{2} reduction such as cutting travel.

title: IT Portfolio
hook: When a question says "classify IT investments by risk and value, then allocate resources optimally", the answer is **IT portfolio**.
model: **IT portfolio**: group IT investments into categories with similar **risk** and **investment value**, then allocate money and people to get the best overall mix, like an investment portfolio.
**Enterprise architecture (EA)**: models the whole organization (business, data, applications, technology) to guide overall optimization.
**Benchmarking**: compare your practices with the best performers to find improvements.
**3C analysis**: look at Customer, Competitor and Company to plan strategy.

example.q: A CIO has 10 proposed IT projects and a fixed budget. How does IT portfolio help?
steps: Sort projects into categories, e.g. low-risk efficiency upgrades vs high-risk new-business systems.
Judge expected value and risk for each category.
Split the budget across categories so total value is high and risk stays balanced.

checks.q: Match each technique to its purpose.
pairs: Allocate IT investment across risk/value categories
Model the whole organization's business and systems
checks.why: Only IT portfolio is about categorizing investments by risk and value to decide resource allocation.

checks.q: A bank sorts its planned IT spending into "keep the lights on", "improve" and "experimental" groups by risk, then sets a budget for each. This is:
checks.why: Grouping investments by risk/value and setting budgets for each group is IT portfolio management.

trap: Enterprise architecture also sounds strategic, but it models the organization's structure. It does not allocate investment by risk.

title: Machine Learning & Deep Learning
hook: FE asks you to spot which scenario really uses ML or DL. The key test: does the system **learn from data**, or was it simply programmed or told the rules?
model: **Machine learning (ML)**: the computer finds patterns in data and improves by itself, without step-by-step programming of the rules.
**Deep learning (DL)**: a type of ML using **multi-layer neural networks**. It needs lots of data (e.g. many images) and is strong at image and speech recognition.
**Expert system**: humans enter expert knowledge as rules, and the computer infers from them. Nothing is learned from data, so it is **not** ML.
Not ML: a fixed sensor trigger, a cause-tree analysis done by people, or the experience curve (costs drop as cumulative output grows).

example.q: A warehouse robot gets faster at picking items. Is this ML?
steps: If engineers rewrote its program each week, that is ordinary programming, not ML.
If the robot improves from its own trial data with no new program, it is learning from data, so it is **ML**.
If that learning used a deep neural network trained on thousands of camera images, it is also **DL**.

checks.q: Which is an example of deep learning?
opts: A thermostat turns on the fan above 30°C
A camera app trained on millions of photos gets better at recognizing faces
Experts write if-then rules for diagnosing engine faults
Workers get faster as total output doubles
checks.why: Training a neural network on a huge set of images to improve recognition is classic DL. A, C and D involve no learning from data.

checks.q: Does the system learn from data?
items: Spam filter improves from emails users mark as spam
Expert system using rules entered by doctors
Airbag fires when the accelerometer passes a threshold
Shop recommends items based on past purchase patterns
checks.why: ML improves from data. Fixed rules and fixed thresholds stay the same no matter how much data passes through.

trap: An expert system sounds intelligent, but its knowledge is entered by humans, not learned from data.

title: Process Mining
hook: FE contrasts process mining with data mining. The giveaway word is **event logs**.
model: **Process mining**: pulls knowledge from IT systems' **event logs** (who did which step, and when) to discover, check and improve real business processes.
It can rebuild the actual process flow, compare it with the intended one, and find bottlenecks.
**Data mining**: uses statistics or AI on large data sets to find unknown patterns or relationships, not process flows.
**BPR**: a radical redesign of processes. It is a management approach, not a log-analysis technique.

example.q: An insurer's claims system logs every step with a timestamp. Managers want to see how claims really move and where they wait. What technique?
steps: The input is event logs: case ID, activity and time.
Analyzing those logs rebuilds the real flow and shows waiting times between steps.
That is **process mining**.

checks.q: A hospital analyzes timestamped system logs to find that patients wait longest between lab tests and doctor review. This is:
checks.why: Rebuilding and analyzing a business process from system event logs is process mining.

checks.q: Process mining or data mining?
items: Finds that shoppers who buy diapers often buy beer
Rebuilds the real order-to-delivery flow from ERP logs
Checks if staff skipped an approval step
Groups customers into segments by spending
checks.why: Process mining works on the steps of a process taken from event logs. Data mining finds patterns in the data itself.

trap: "Finding unsuspected relationships in data sets" describes data mining, not process mining.

title: System Procurement Steps (RFI → RFP)
hook: FE shows the procurement flow with a blank. Remember **I before P**: get information first, then ask for proposals.
model: **RFI (Request for Information)**: the orderer shares its goals and business details and asks vendors for information about available technology and solutions.
**RFP (Request for Proposal)**: the orderer states the target system and procurement conditions and asks vendors to submit **proposals**.
**Select the vendor**: evaluate the proposals and vendor capabilities, then choose the procurement source.
**Conclude a contract**: both sides confirm roles and responsibilities in writing.

example.q: A city government wants a new permit system. Put its actions in order.
steps: Ask vendors what solutions exist (**RFI**).
Send the requirements and terms and ask for proposals (**RFP**).
Compare proposals and pick a vendor.
Sign a contract stating each side's responsibilities.

checks.q: Put the procurement steps in order.
steps: Request for information (RFI)
Request for proposal (RFP)
Evaluate proposals and select a vendor
Conclude a contract
checks.why: You need information to write good requirements. You need proposals to choose a vendor, and the contract comes last.

checks.q: An orderer gives vendors the target system's requirements and conditions and asks each to submit a proposal document. This step is:
checks.why: Asking for a proposal against stated requirements is the RFP. An RFI only asks for information.

trap: RFI is the earlier step (asking for information). A request for a **proposal** is the RFP.

title: SCM & ERP
hook: These two, plus CRM, SFA and knowledge management, show up as a matching game. Each one has a clear keyword.
model: **SCM (Supply Chain Management)**: looks at the whole chain (purchasing, production, distribution, sales) **across companies** for total optimization, cutting lead time and inventory.

**ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning)**: plans and controls a company's management resources (people, goods, money, information) company-wide. An **ERP package** puts core tasks (production, accounting, sales, HR, payroll) on **one integrated database**.
**CRM**: combines customer data from many channels to build long-term customer relationships.
**SFA**: uses IT to make sales activities more efficient.
**Knowledge management**: shares individuals' know-how across the organization.

example.q: A maker, its parts suppliers and its retailers share sales and stock data so every party orders just enough. Which concept?
steps: Several companies are involved, from suppliers through to retailers.
The goal is less inventory and shorter delivery time for the chain as a whole.
That is **SCM**. ERP would cover resources inside a single company.

checks.q: Match each concept to its focus.
pairs: Integrate company-wide resources in one system
Make sales staff's work more efficient with IT
checks.why: Keywords: chain/across companies = SCM, whole company's resources = ERP, customers = CRM, sales activities = SFA.

checks.q: A firm replaces separate accounting, payroll and production systems with one package sharing a single database. This is:
checks.why: Bringing core business functions together in one integrated database for company-wide resource planning is ERP.

trap: If the question stresses **between companies** and inventory/lead time, it's SCM. **Company-wide** resource integration is ERP.

title: Smart Meter & Smart Grid
hook: Easy marks if you remember that "grid" means the electricity network and a smart meter measures and communicates. It does not store power.
model: **Smart meter**: a digital electricity meter with **communication** and device-control functions.
Smart meter uses: **automatic meter reading**, showing (visualizing) power usage to encourage saving, and **demand response**, which cuts peak demand by controlling usage.
A smart meter is **not** a battery or backup power source.
**Smart grid**: an electricity network that uses ICT to control **generation and consumption together**. This helps bring in renewable energy, keeps supply stable and balances demand.

example.q: During a heat wave, a utility signals homes to delay running water heaters, and home meters respond. What is happening?
steps: The utility lowers peak demand by controlling consumption. That is **demand response**.
Home **smart meters** receive the signal and report the usage.
The network that coordinates generation and consumption this way is a **smart grid**.

checks.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a smart meter?
opts: Showing households their real-time power use
Supplying power to the home during an outage
checks.why: A smart meter measures, communicates and controls. It has no energy storage, so it cannot act as backup power.

checks.q: Device or network?
items: Installed at each home to measure and send usage data
Integrates control of power plants and consumers with ICT
Lets the utility read meters without visiting
Helps absorb variable solar and wind generation
checks.why: The meter is the endpoint at each customer. The grid is the whole ICT-controlled power network.

trap: Demand response sounds too advanced to be a meter feature, but it is a real smart-meter purpose. Backup power is the one that's false.

title: Audit Checkpoints & CIA
hook: Audit questions give a risk and ask for the matching checkpoint; first classify the risk.
model: A **system audit** is an independent check of controls over information systems, with advice for improvement.
A checkpoint must address the **exact risk** stated.
**Confidentiality** (only authorized access): encryption, access control, banning media removal.
**Integrity** (accurate, complete): input error checks, change control.
**Availability** (usable when needed): redundancy, backups, SLA on downtime.
Risk 'user requirements not met' in design → **user department reviews** design documents.

example.q: Risk: system documents leak or are misused. Checkpoint?
steps: Leakage/misuse = unauthorized access.
That is a **confidentiality** risk.
Checkpoint: measures that keep the documents confidential.

checks.q: Which CIA element does each control mainly protect?
items: Encrypting the customer database
Validation checks on input forms
Clustered servers with failover
Login access rights per role
Monitoring downtime against the SLA
checks.why: Secrecy = C, correctness = I, uptime = A.

checks.q: Risk: programs do not match the system design. Which checkpoint fits?
opts: Program specs are prepared based on the design documents
checks.why: Design-to-program consistency is checked by tracing specs to design; user review targets unmet requirements.

trap: Input error checking sounds like security, but it protects integrity, not availability.

title: Capacity Management Techniques
hook: Expect a question that describes a technique and asks its name: trend analysis, analytical modeling, simulation, or baselining.
model: Capacity management makes sure capacity and performance meet current and future agreed needs at justified cost.
**Trend analysis**: track a resource's usage over time and extrapolate future usage.
**Analytical modeling**: math such as **queueing theory** to predict response time/throughput.
**Simulation modeling**: run simulated (synthetic) transactions to predict performance.
**Baseline model**: first build a model that matches current performance.

example.q: CPU use rose 5% a month for a year. When does it hit 90%?
steps: Data is a time series of one resource.
Extending the line into the future = **trend analysis**.
Use the forecast to plan an upgrade before 90%.

checks.q: Match the technique to its description.
checks.why: Trend = history over time; analytical = math; simulation = synthetic load; baseline = today's reference model.

checks.q: A team feeds made-up transactions to a model of the system to estimate throughput. This is:
checks.why: Generating simulated transactions is simulation; trend analysis uses real usage history.

trap: Simulation also predicts the future, but trend analysis is the one built on chronological usage data.

title: Outsourcing Risks & Measures
hook: Outsourcing questions name a risk and ask which measure targets it; match the measure to that exact risk.
model: Quality decline → agree a target **service level (SLA)** and track quality indicators to drive improvement.
Unclear or high cost → state the fee structure per service; keep in-house staff who can judge costs.
Information leakage → confidentiality clauses, access control, audits of the vendor.
Loss of in-house know-how / vendor lock-in → keep key skills and documentation in-house.

example.q: After outsourcing operations, response times are slipping. Best measure?
steps: Risk named: decline in service **quality**.
Measure that controls quality: agreed service levels + KPIs reviewed regularly.
Fee details or training plans don't directly fix quality.

checks.q: Which risk does each measure address?
items: Agree service levels and monitor KPIs
Itemize fees per service in the contract
Add a nondisclosure clause
Keep staff able to judge cost validity
checks.why: Each measure only controls the risk it targets.

checks.q: Which SLA element best lets the client check service quality?
opts: Measurable service level targets, e.g. response time
checks.why: Quality is controlled through measurable, agreed targets.

trap: Picking a reasonable long-term measure (like an HR plan) that doesn't target the risk asked.

title: Incident vs Problem Management
hook: FE asks how incidents and problems relate: who restores service, who finds the root cause, and how the records link.
model: **Incident management**: restore normal service ASAP (a workaround is fine).
**Problem management**: find the **root cause** of one or more incidents and prevent recurrence.
A problem record **cross-references** its incidents; one problem can link to **many** incidents.
**Known error**: a problem whose root cause (and workaround) has been identified and documented.
Incident records are kept, not deleted, when the problem is closed.

example.q: Ten users report the same app crash this week. What happens?
steps: Service desk logs 10 incidents and gives a restart workaround.
Problem management opens **one** problem record linked to all 10.
Root cause found (memory leak) → recorded as a known error.
A change request applies the permanent fix.

checks.q: Incident or problem management?
items: Give the user a workaround so work continues
Analyze why the same crash keeps happening
Restore service within the SLA target time
Record a known error
checks.why: Incident = fast restoration; problem = root cause and prevention.

checks.q: Which is true of problem records?
opts: They hold links to the incidents that triggered them
Each one is tied to exactly one incident
Linked incidents are deleted once the cause is known
checks.why: The cross-reference ties the processes together; one problem may cover many incidents, and records are retained.

trap: Thinking one problem = one incident; a single root cause often explains many incidents.

title: RTO, RPO and MTD
hook: Disaster-recovery questions test which objective measures what, and how they must relate: recovery has to finish before the business can no longer survive.
model: **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective): the point in time data is restored to = how much data loss is acceptable. Backup interval must not exceed it.
**RTO** (Recovery Time Objective): target time to restore the service after the disruption.
**MTD** (Maximum Tolerable Downtime): the longest outage the business can survive.
Rule: **RTO < MTD**; otherwise the business fails before recovery ends.

example.q: MTD is 24 h. Recovery: 3 h to declare a disaster, 5 h to set up the backup site, 8 h to restore data. Is the plan OK?
steps: Compare: 16 h < 24 h MTD.
Plan is OK with 24 − 16 = **8 h** of margin.

checks.q: Match each term to what it limits.
pairs: How much recent data may be lost
How long restoring the service may take
How long the business can survive an outage
checks.why: RPO looks back from the incident (data), RTO looks forward (recovery time), MTD is the business survival limit.

checks.q: MTD is 36 h. Steps: 4 h detect and decide, 10 h switch to the standby site, 6 h verify data. Hours of margin left before MTD?
Backups run every 4 hours. Which objective does this interval mainly support?
checks.why: The backup interval sets the worst-case data loss, which is the RPO.

trap: RPO is about lost data, not recovery time, so 'RPO < MTD' is not the required relation.

title: SLA Availability & Allowed Downtime
hook: A favorite calculation: given the service hours and an SLA availability %, find the maximum downtime per month.
model: **Availability** = (agreed service time − downtime) ÷ agreed service time.
Agreed service time counts **only the service window** × business days, not 24 h.
Max downtime = (1 − availability) × agreed service time.
Agreed planned maintenance is usually excluded from service time.

example.q: Service runs 9:00 AM–9:00 PM, 25 business days, SLA 99.8%. Max downtime?
steps: Window = 12 h/day.
Service time = 12 × 25 = 300 h.

checks.q: Service hours 6:00 AM–6:00 PM, 20 business days a month, SLA availability 99%. Max downtime per month in hours?
checks.why: 12 h × 20 = 240 h of service; 1% of 240 = 2.4 h.

checks.q: A service had 400 agreed hours last month and was down 2 h. Availability in %?
Which figure should you multiply by (1 − availability) to get the allowed downtime?
opts: Agreed service hours in the period
Number of incidents in the month
checks.why: The SLA promises availability only during the agreed window, so only those hours count.

trap: Using 24 h/day instead of the service window gives a downtime that is too big.

title: COCOMO Cost Model
hook: The exam checks that you know which way COCOMO works: software size goes in, effort and duration come out.
model: **COCOMO** (Constructive Cost Model) is a **cost model** that uses a statistical formula.
Input: estimated software **size** (thousands of lines of code, KLOC).
Output: **effort** (person-months), then the project **duration** (months).
Three levels: **basic**, **intermediate**, **detailed**.
Average staff = effort ÷ duration.

example.q: A system is sized at 40 KLOC. Using COCOMO, the formula gives 120 person-months and a duration of 12 months. What is the average team size?
steps: Size (40 KLOC) is the input to the formula.
The formula outputs effort = 120 person-months and duration = 12 months.
Average staff = 120 ÷ 12 = **10 people**.

checks.q: A team knows only the estimated KLOC of a new system. What does COCOMO let them work out?
opts: Effort, from the planned end date
checks.why: Size is the known starting point; effort and duration are what the model calculates.

checks.q: COCOMO estimates 48 person-months of effort and a duration of 8 months. What is the average number of staff?
checks.why: Average staff = effort ÷ duration = 48 ÷ 8 = **6**.

trap: Reversing the direction: COCOMO never derives size from effort; size is the input.

title: Critical Path (Arrow Diagram)
hook: Arrow-diagram questions ask for the critical path or the minimum project length; one missed dummy arrow gives the wrong answer.
model: The **critical path** is the **longest** path from start to end; its length is the minimum project duration.
Activities on it have **no slack**: any delay delays the whole project.
Forward pass: at a merge node, take the **largest** earliest time.
A **dummy** (dashed arrow) takes 0 days but still forces the waiting activity to start later.
Shortening a non-critical activity does not shorten the project.

example.q: A (3 days) starts the project. B (4) and C (7) follow A. D (2) follows B. E (1) needs both C and D finished. Find the critical path.
steps: E can start only at max(3+7, 3+4+2) = max(10, 9) = 10.
Longest path = **A-C-E, 11 days**; path B-D has 1 day of slack.

checks.q: P (5 days) starts the project. Q (8) and R (3) follow P. S (4) follows R. T (2) needs both Q and S finished. What is the minimum project duration?
checks.why: P-Q-T = 5 + 8 + 2 = 15; P-R-S-T = 5 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 14. The longest path decides: **15 days**.

checks.q: In that same project, R is shortened by 1 day. What is the new project duration?
checks.why: R is not on the critical path (P-Q-T), so cutting it only adds slack. The project still takes 15 days.

trap: Ignoring a dummy arrow, which hides a dependency and makes a shorter path look critical.

title: Effort Estimation from Function Points
hook: Effort questions chain a few small steps; most wrong answers come from skipping the overhead added at the end.
model: The **FP (function point) method** measures size by counting inputs, outputs, inquiries, logical files and interfaces, with weights.
Development effort = FP ÷ productivity (FP per person-month).
Add the other fixed work (e.g. installation, training).
When an overhead is a percentage of **all** the other work (as project management usually is in these questions), apply it to the **sum**, so add it last.

example.q: 300 FP, productivity 15 FP per person-month, 5 person-months for installation, plus 20% for project management. Total effort?
steps: Development = 300 ÷ 15 = 20 person-months.
Add installation: 20 + 5 = 25.
Add 20% PM: 25 × 1.2 = **30 person-months**.

checks.q: 800 FP, productivity 20 FP per person-month, 8 person-months for testing and training, and project management adds 25% of all that work. Total person-months?
checks.why: 800 ÷ 20 = 40; 40 + 8 = 48; 48 × 1.25 = **60**. Stopping at 48 forgets the PM overhead.

checks.q: Put the calculation steps in order.
steps: Divide FP by productivity
Add fixed work such as installation
Apply the percentage overhead to the total
checks.why: The overhead is a percentage of all the other work, so it must come after everything else is added.

trap: Forgetting to add the percentage overhead, or applying it to development effort only when the question says it covers all the work.

title: Earned Value Management (EVM)
hook: EVM questions either ask you to define PV, EV or AC, or give you the three figures and ask if the project is over budget, behind schedule, or both.
model: **PV** (Planned Value): budget for the work **scheduled** to be done by now.
**EV** (Earned Value): budget for the work **actually completed** so far.
**AC** (Actual Cost): money **really spent** on the completed work.
**CV** = `EV − AC` (cost) and **SV** = `EV − PV` (schedule). Negative = over budget / behind schedule.
**CPI** = `EV ÷ AC` and **SPI** = `EV ÷ PV`. Below 1 is bad, above 1 is good.

example.q: PV = `$100,000`, EV = `$90,000`, AC = `$120,000`. How is the project doing?
steps: Both indices < 1: over budget **and** behind schedule.

checks.q: Match each EVM term to its meaning.
pairs: Budget for the work planned to be done by now
Budget value of the work actually finished
Real cost spent on the work finished
checks.why: PV is the plan, EV is what the finished work is worth in budget terms, and AC is the money really spent.

checks.q: EV = `$60,000` and AC = `$75,000`. What is the CPI?
checks.why: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 60,000 ÷ 75,000 = **0.8**. Each $1 spent earned only $0.80 of value, so the project is over budget.

trap: Mixing up the three values: the budget for **planned** work is PV and the **real cost** is AC; only the budget for **completed** work is EV.

title: PERT Three-Point Estimate
hook: You get an optimistic, most likely and pessimistic figure and must apply the weighted PERT formula, not a plain average.
model: Three estimates: **O** (optimistic, best case), **M** (most likely, normal case), **P** (pessimistic, worst case).
PERT (beta distribution) expected value = `(O + 4M + P) ÷ 6`.
M is weighted **4 times**; the total weight is 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.
Works for time or cost.

example.q: A task costs `$20,000` at best, `$30,000` normally and `$58,000` at worst. Expected cost?

checks.q: A task takes 4 days at best, 7 days normally and 16 days at worst. What is the PERT expected duration?
checks.why: (4 + 4×7 + 16) ÷ 6 = (4 + 28 + 16) ÷ 6 = 48 ÷ 6 = **8 days**. A plain average would give 9.

checks.q: Match each term to its role in the formula.
checks.why: Expected = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6: the weights 1, 4, 1 add up to 6.

trap: Taking the simple average (O + M + P) ÷ 3, which ignores the 4× weight on the most likely value.

title: Scope Management
hook: The exam describes a goal and asks which project management subject group it belongs to; scope is about what the project will and will not deliver.
model: **Scope**: define objectives, deliverables, requirements and **boundaries** (what is in and out).
Scope also controls **changes** to the deliverables, so their effect on the project is managed.
The **WBS** (Work Breakdown Structure) breaks the deliverables into smaller work packages.
Compare: **Risk** = uncertain events; **Procurement** = buying from suppliers.

example.q: A client asks to add a mobile app halfway through a web project. Which subject group handles the request?
steps: The request changes a project **deliverable**.
Deciding if it is in or out, and handling its impact, is change control on the boundaries.
So it is **scope** management.

checks.q: Match each subject group to its purpose.
pairs: Set deliverables and boundaries; control changes to them
Identify and respond to uncertain events
Obtain goods and services from suppliers
checks.why: Only scope is about what the project delivers and where its boundaries are.

checks.q: A team lists which features are excluded from the project and reviews every request to change the deliverables. Which subject group is this?
checks.why: Exclusions are boundaries and deliverable changes are scope control. Risk deals with uncertain events, not deliverable changes.

trap: Choosing Risk because the purpose mentions positive and negative impacts; when the impact comes from changes to deliverables, it is Scope.

title: Break-Even & Target Profit
hook: Units to break even or to earn a target profit is a classic: add the target profit to fixed costs.
model: **Break-even point**: sales = total cost (fixed + variable), so profit = 0.
Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit.
Break-even units = fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit.
Target-profit units = (fixed cost + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit.
Break-even sales = fixed cost ÷ (1 − variable cost ratio).

example.q: Price $25, variable cost $15/unit, fixed cost $60,000. Units for $20,000 profit?
steps: Contribution = 25 − 15 = $10.
Break-even = 60,000 ÷ 10 = 6,000 units.

checks.q: Price $50, variable cost $30/unit, fixed costs $100,000. Units needed for a $40,000 profit?
Fixed costs $300,000; variable cost ratio 0.4. Break-even sales ($)?
Interest expense and admin salaries that don't change with volume are:
checks.why: Costs that stay constant regardless of units sold are fixed; add them all up first.

trap: Stopping at break-even (fixed ÷ contribution) and forgetting to add the target profit.

title: Development Cost Comparison
hook: You compare options (buy, outsource, build) by totaling every cost item; the cheapest-looking single number is often a trap.
model: Total cost = purchase + outsourcing + labor.
Labor per process = persons × months × cost per person-month.
Use each process's own duration and rate.
Compute **every** option fully before choosing.

example.q: A: buy $50,000 + 2 persons × 3 months × $8,000. B: outsource $120,000. Cheaper?
steps: B = $120,000 → **A** is cheaper.

checks.q: X: buy $30,000 + 3 persons × 2 months × $7,000. Y: outsource $80,000. Z: build 5 persons × 3 months × $4,000, then test 1 person × 2 months × $7,000. Lowest total cost ($)?
Order the steps to compare options.
steps: List each option's cost items
Compute labor = persons × months × rate per process
Add purchase, outsourcing and labor
Pick the lowest total
checks.why: Only after full totals are known can you compare fairly.

trap: Choosing the single lump-sum option without adding up the in-house labor of the others.

title: Financial Statements
hook: Know which statement shows a snapshot vs a period, and how the profit levels are derived.
model: **Balance sheet (B/S)**: assets, liabilities, net assets (capital) at **one point in time**.
**Income statement (P/L)**: revenues, expenses and profit over **a period**.
**Cash flow statement**: cash in/out over a period (operating, investing, financing).
**Statement of changes in equity**: how net assets changed during the period.
Gross profit = sales − cost of sales; operating income = gross profit − SG&A; ordinary profit = operating income + non-operating income − non-operating expenses.

example.q: Sales 1,000; cost of sales 600; SG&A 250; non-op income 20; non-op expense 30. Ordinary profit?
steps: Operating = 400 − 250 = 150.

checks.q: Match the statement to what it shows.
pairs: Financial position on a given date
Profit or loss for the period
checks.why: Only the B/S is a point-in-time snapshot; the others cover a period.

checks.q: Sales 800; cost of sales 500; SG&A 180. Operating income?

trap: The income statement also reports results, but over a period, not as a snapshot of assets and liabilities.

title: Software Licenses & Patent Cross-Licensing
hook: Short definition items: when a license contract is formed, and what kind of arrangement shares patents.
model: **Shrink-wrap license**: terms are shown on the package; opening (breaking the wrap) = accepting.
**Click-wrap license**: accepted by clicking 'I agree' during install/download.
**Patent cross-licensing**: companies mutually license each other's patents in specified fields.
**Open source**: source code published; anyone may modify and redistribute under the license.
**Site license**: one contract lets an organization use the software on many machines.

example.q: A buyer receives a boxed DVD and tears off the wrap. When is the contract made?
steps: The package states that opening it means agreement.
Payment or delivery isn't the trigger.
Contract concluded **when the package is opened**.

checks.q: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: Firms permit use of each other's patents
checks.why: Each is defined by how or between whom rights are granted.

checks.q: Two chip makers agree each may use the other's patents for memory products. This is:
checks.why: Mutual permission to use patents in a defined field is cross-licensing.

trap: Shrink-wrap is not at installation; that is click-wrap.

title: Standards Organizations
hook: Know which bodies set international vs national standards; WTO-related questions point to international ones.
model: **ISO**: international standards in general, including IT (with IEC).
**IEC**: international, electrical/electronic; **ITU-T**: international, telecommunications.
**ANSI** (US) and **BSI** (UK) are **national** standards bodies.
**FCC** is a US government regulator for communications, not an international standard.
WTO's TBT agreement asks members to base technical rules on **international standards** (e.g. ISO).

example.q: A product is for government buyers in many WTO countries. Which standards?
steps: Many countries → national standards won't fit all.
WTO members base rules on international standards.
Choose **ISO**.

checks.q: International or national body?
items: ISO
ANSI
ITU-T
BSI
IEC
checks.why: ISO, IEC and ITU-T are international; ANSI (US) and BSI (UK) are national.

checks.q: Which body mainly standardizes telecommunications worldwide?
checks.why: ITU-T is the telecom standardization sector of the ITU, an international organization.

trap: ANSI is famous, but it is the US national body, not an international one.

title: Straight-Line Depreciation
hook: A quick calculation item: subtract the residual value before dividing by the useful life.
model: **Depreciation** spreads a fixed asset's cost over its useful life as an expense.
Straight-line: (acquisition cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, the same amount every year.
Book value after n years = cost − n × annual depreciation.
Declining-balance instead multiplies the book value by a fixed rate.

example.q: Machine costs $85,000, residual $5,000, life 8 years. Annual depreciation?
steps: Depreciable amount = 85,000 − 5,000 = 80,000.
Book value after 3 years = 85,000 − 30,000 = $55,000.

checks.q: Server bought for $48,000, residual value $3,000, useful life 5 years. Annual straight-line depreciation ($)?
Same server: book value ($) at the end of year 2?
Which method charges the same depreciation every year?
checks.why: Declining-balance applies a rate to a shrinking book value, so its charge falls each year.

trap: Dividing the full cost by the life (forgetting the residual value) gives a too-large figure.
